articles.title: Rare footage captured of Great White shark in Mediterranean Sea
articles.summaryB1:
A volunteer diver had an incredible and frightening experience when he filmed a Great White shark in the Mediterranean Sea. The encounter happened in the waters between Tunisia, a country in North Africa, and Sicily, an island in southern Italy. The diver said he was shaking while he recorded the rare footage of the shark underwater.

Great White sharks are endangered animals, which means there are very few of them left in the world. Seeing one in the Mediterranean Sea is very unusual. Scientists and wildlife experts say that Great White sharks rarely appear in this part of the world, so this video is very important.

The footage that the diver captured is now helping people learn more about these animals and where they live. Great White sharks are often seen as dangerous, but they are also a protected species because their numbers have fallen so much over the years.

Many people are excited about the video because it shows that Great White sharks still exist in the Mediterranean. Conservation groups hope that rare sightings like this one will help the public understand why it is important to protect these animals. The diver was brave to keep filming even though he was afraid. His video gives scientists a valuable chance to study the behaviour of this endangered creature in its natural habitat.

vocabularyB1.definition: A person who does work without being paid, by their own choice.
At serious risk of disappearing completely from the world.
A recording of something on video or film.
An occasion when someone sees something rare or unusual.
The natural environment where an animal or plant normally lives.

articles.summaryB2:
A volunteer diver has recounted the visceral experience of encountering an endangered Great White shark in the Mediterranean Sea, describing how his hands were shaking as he managed to film the rare creature. The sighting occurred in the stretch of water between Tunisia and Sicily — a region not typically associated with Great White shark activity — making the footage all the more remarkable.

Great White sharks are classified as an endangered species, their populations having declined sharply due to overfishing, habitat loss, and slow reproductive rates. Documented appearances in the Mediterranean are exceptionally uncommon, and marine biologists regard any confirmed sighting in these waters as scientifically significant. The diver's video, captured under what must have been considerable psychological pressure, offers researchers a rare opportunity to examine the species' range and behaviour in a region often overlooked in broader conservation discussions.

The encounter raises broader questions about shifting marine ecosystems and whether environmental changes may be prompting these apex predators to venture into less familiar territories. Conservation advocates argue that high-profile incidents like this one can galvanise public interest in protecting a species that, despite its fearsome reputation, is itself under serious threat.

While the diver's instinct might understandably have been to retreat, his resolve to keep filming has yielded a document of genuine ecological value — a reminder that citizen science, however unintentional, can make a meaningful contribution to our understanding of the natural world.

vocabularyB2.definition: Based on deep, instinctive feelings rather than thought; raw and physical.
An animal at the top of the food chain with no natural enemies.
To shock or excite people into taking action about something.
Strong determination to continue doing something despite difficulty.
Relating to the relationship between living things and their environment.

articles.questionB1: Would you be brave enough to keep filming if you had a surprise sighting of an endangered animal? Why or why not?
articles.questionB2: How far can a single piece of footage from an unintentional citizen scientist galvanise public resolve to protect apex predators with a dangerous reputation?

articles.title: 'No dead ends': What the Dutch can teach us about tackling youth unemployment
articles.summaryB1:
Youth unemployment is a big problem in many countries. Young people who are not studying, working, or doing any training are sometimes called 'NEET' – Not in Education, Employment, or Training. Having too many young people in this situation can cause serious problems for society and the economy.

The Netherlands has found very effective ways to tackle this problem. The country has one of the lowest rates of young NEETs in the world, among people aged 16 to 24. This is a great achievement, and other countries want to understand how the Dutch system works.

One important idea in the Netherlands is that young people should never reach a dead end – a situation where they have no options and nowhere to go. The Dutch system tries to make sure there is always a next step available for every young person, whether that is more education, a job, or professional training.

Government support plays a key role in this. Local authorities work closely with young people to find out what they need and help them move forward. Early action is also very important – problems are identified quickly before they become worse.

Other countries could learn a lot from the Dutch approach. When young people have opportunities and support, they can build better futures. This benefits not only the individuals but also the whole of society.

vocabularyB1.definition: The situation of not having a job when you want one
To deal with a difficult problem and try to solve it
Something successful that you have done, often after hard work
A situation with no way forward and no more options
Official organisations or people with power to make decisions

articles.summaryB2:
Youth unemployment remains one of the most persistent socioeconomic challenges facing developed nations, yet the Netherlands has emerged as a striking exception. The country consistently records one of the world's lowest proportions of 16 to 24-year-olds classified as NEET – Not in Education, Employment, or Training – a benchmark increasingly used by policymakers to gauge how effectively societies are integrating young people into productive life.

Central to the Dutch model is a philosophy of ensuring there are, in the words used to describe the approach, 'no dead ends'. Rather than allowing young people to fall through the cracks of bureaucratic systems, the Netherlands has built a framework designed to keep every pathway open. Whether through vocational training, apprenticeships, or targeted employment schemes, the emphasis is on early intervention and personalised support before disengagement becomes entrenched.

Local municipalities play a pivotal role, working proactively to identify at-risk individuals and connect them with appropriate resources. This decentralised approach allows for tailored responses rather than one-size-fits-all policy, arguably one of its greatest strengths.

The implications for other nations are considerable. High NEET rates carry long-term costs – not only for the individuals concerned, whose prospects narrow significantly over time, but for wider society through lost productivity and increased welfare dependency. The Dutch example suggests that sustained investment in youth support systems, combined with structural flexibility, can yield measurable and lasting results.

vocabularyB2.definition: A standard used to measure or compare the quality of something
Action taken early to prevent a problem from getting worse
Deeply fixed and very difficult to change or remove
Extremely important and having a major influence on something
Relying long-term on government financial support instead of working

articles.questionB1: If your country wanted to tackle youth unemployment like the Netherlands, what changes do you think would be the biggest achievement?
articles.questionB2: To what extent do you think early intervention and decentralised support are enough to prevent welfare dependency, or are there deeper structural barriers the Dutch model cannot address?

articles.title: Next El Niño could be strongest in decades
articles.summaryB1: The United Nations has warned that a new El Niño weather event could begin very soon, possibly within just a few weeks. El Niño is a natural weather pattern that happens in the Pacific Ocean. It occurs when ocean water becomes warmer than usual, and this change affects weather all around the world. El Niño can cause serious problems such as heavy rainfall in some regions and drought in others. Scientists are concerned because our planet is already experiencing the effects of climate change, which has been making temperatures rise for many years. When El Niño combines with climate change, the result could be even more extreme weather than normal. The UN believes this new phase could be one of the strongest El Niño events in decades. This is worrying for many countries because extreme weather can damage homes, destroy crops, and affect millions of people. Governments and scientists are monitoring the situation closely so they can warn communities in advance. It is important for people to understand that natural events like El Niño and human-caused climate change can work together to boost temperatures to dangerous levels. Experts say that reducing carbon emissions remains essential to limit future risks. This story reminds us why protecting our environment matters so much.

vocabularyB1.definition: A long period with very little or no rain, causing water shortages.
Very unusual and dangerous weather conditions, such as floods or heatwaves.
A stage or period in a process or cycle.
To watch or check something carefully over a period of time.
To increase or raise something to a higher level.

articles.summaryB2: The United Nations has issued a warning that a new El Niño cycle could emerge within weeks, raising fears that global temperatures — already elevated by decades of human-driven climate change — may climb to unprecedented levels. El Niño is a naturally occurring climatic phenomenon originating in the Pacific Ocean, characterised by an unusual warming of surface waters that disrupts atmospheric circulation patterns worldwide. Its consequences typically include intensified rainfall across parts of South America, severe drought across sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia, and heightened hurricane activity in certain ocean basins. What makes this potential episode particularly alarming is its projected intensity. Scientists suggest it could rank among the most powerful El Niño events in several decades, a prospect that compounds existing anxieties about a planet already under considerable environmental strain. The convergence of a strong El Niño with the underlying warming trend driven by greenhouse gas emissions could push annual mean temperatures to record-breaking highs, with cascading effects on food security, water availability, and public health in vulnerable regions. Climate scientists emphasise that while El Niño is a natural phenomenon, its destructive potential is amplified by anthropogenic climate change, making adaptation strategies more urgent than ever. Authorities and humanitarian organisations are being urged to prepare contingency plans, as early warning systems may provide only a narrow window in which to act. The episode serves as a stark reminder of the accelerating intersection between natural climate variability and human-induced environmental disruption.

vocabularyB2.definition: Never having happened before; at a level or scale not previously recorded.
The coming together of two or more different things at the same point or time.
Caused or produced by human activity, especially in relation to environmental damage.
A series of consequences where one event triggers further connected problems.
Plans prepared in advance to deal with a possible emergency or unexpected situation.

articles.questionB1: When extreme weather events like El Niño happen more often, how should governments monitor and protect vulnerable communities?
articles.questionB2: Given the convergence of El Niño and anthropogenic climate change, how effective can contingency plans realistically be when the warning window is so narrow?

articles.title: I wanted to quit Eurovision twice - then won it, says Bangaranga singer Dara
articles.summaryB1:
A Bulgarian singer named Dara has won the Eurovision Song Contest 2025 in Vienna with her song 'Bangaranga'. But her victory almost did not happen. Dara says she wanted to quit the competition twice before she finally won it. This makes her story very special and inspiring.

Eurovision is a huge international singing competition where countries from across Europe and beyond send one artist or group to perform a song. Millions of people watch it every year on television. Winning Eurovision is a very big achievement for any singer.

For Bulgaria, this victory is historic. It is the first time the country has won the contest. Before this win, Bulgaria had taken part in Eurovision many times but had never finished in first place. This makes Dara's win even more important for her country.

Dara has not spoken in detail about why she wanted to quit, but she has said that the journey was very difficult. Despite the challenges she faced, she decided to continue and perform. In the end, her determination paid off and she received enough votes to become the winner.

Her story shows that giving up is not always the right choice. Sometimes, continuing through difficult moments can lead to great success. Dara is now celebrating her historic win and Bulgaria is very proud of her achievement.

vocabularyB1.definition: A win; success in a competition or battle
To stop doing something; to give up
Very important and remembered in history; happening for the first time
A strong decision to keep trying even when something is hard
Something important and difficult that you have successfully done

articles.summaryB2:
Bulgarian singer Dara has claimed a landmark victory at the Eurovision Song Contest 2025 in Vienna, winning with her entry 'Bangaranga' — but according to the artist herself, the triumph came perilously close to never materialising. Dara has revealed that she considered withdrawing from the competition on two separate occasions before ultimately going on to claim the top prize.

The disclosure adds a compelling layer of human drama to what is already a historically significant result. It marks the first time Bulgaria has ever won the Eurovision Song Contest, a milestone that will resonate deeply with the country's music fans and cultural commentators alike. The competition, which attracts television audiences of hundreds of millions across Europe and beyond, is widely regarded as one of the most prestigious platforms in popular music.

While Dara has not elaborated extensively on the precise reasons behind her impulse to walk away, her candid admission speaks to the immense psychological pressure that competing on such a vast international stage can place on performers. Her decision to persevere despite those doubts has, in hindsight, proven to be defining.

Dara's win is likely to spark renewed interest in Bulgarian participation in future Eurovision cycles and may elevate her profile significantly on the European music scene. Her story also serves as a broader reminder that resilience in the face of self-doubt can ultimately prove transformative, both for an individual artist and for their nation's cultural standing.

vocabularyB2.definition: Very important and significant; marking a major moment in history
Very dangerously; in a way that was almost a serious problem
Honest and open, especially about personal or difficult things
To keep trying hard even when something is very difficult
The ability to recover and keep going after difficulties or setbacks

articles.questionB1: Dara showed great determination to continue despite wanting to quit twice. Can you think of a time when you or someone you know kept going through difficulty?
articles.questionB2: Dara's candid admission about nearly withdrawing adds human drama to her landmark win. How do you think public vulnerability affects the way audiences connect with artists?

articles.title: The gamers taking on the industry to stop it switching off games
articles.summaryB1:
A group of gamers is fighting against big video game companies. They want to stop companies from turning off online games permanently. When a company shuts down a game's servers, players can no longer play it, even if they paid a lot of money for it. This makes many people very angry.

The campaign is called Stop Killing Games. It is asking governments to create new rules that would force publishers to keep games playable after they close the official servers. For example, they want companies to release special software so players can run the game themselves.

This is becoming a bigger problem because many modern games need an internet connection to work. If the company decides to shut down the servers, the game simply stops working forever. Players feel this is unfair because they own the game but cannot use it.

The campaign has already collected hundreds of thousands of signatures across Europe. Supporters argue that when you buy something, you should be able to keep using it. Publishers, however, say that running servers costs money and they cannot do it forever.

This debate raises an important question about digital ownership. Do you really own a game if a company can switch it off? Many players believe that consumers deserve better protection. The outcome of this campaign could change how the gaming industry works in the future.

vocabularyB1.definition: Powerful computers that store data and let people connect to online games or websites
Companies that produce and sell video games to the public
An organised effort by a group of people to achieve a goal or change something
People's names written or collected to show support for an idea or request
People who buy and use products or services

articles.summaryB2:
A grassroots movement known as Stop Killing Games is mounting a significant challenge to the established practices of the video game industry, specifically targeting the widespread phenomenon of publishers permanently deactivating titles without ensuring any form of continued playability for consumers.

The core grievance is straightforward yet legally complex: when a publisher shuts down the servers that power an online game, the product becomes entirely non-functional, regardless of how much players originally paid for it. Critics argue this constitutes a fundamental breach of consumer rights, drawing a sharp distinction between merely discontinuing support and actively rendering a purchased product inoperable.

The campaign has gained considerable traction across Europe, amassing hundreds of thousands of signatures in support of regulatory intervention. Campaigners are not necessarily demanding that publishers maintain servers indefinitely; rather, they are calling for legislation that would compel companies to release tools or patches enabling players to host games independently once official support ends.

The movement touches on deeper tensions around digital ownership. Unlike physical media, digital products can be revoked or disabled remotely, raising uncomfortable questions about what consumers actually acquire when they purchase a game. Supporters contend that stronger legal safeguards are long overdue.

Publishers, for their part, point to the prohibitive ongoing costs of server maintenance as justification for eventual shutdowns. Nevertheless, the momentum behind Stop Killing Games suggests that regulators may soon be forced to scrutinise industry practices that have, until now, gone largely unchallenged.

vocabularyB2.definition: An organised effort started by ordinary people rather than governments or large organisations
Growing support, attention, or progress towards achieving a goal
Action taken by a government or official body to control or change an industry's behaviour
No longer able to function or be used; completely broken or disabled
To examine something very carefully and critically, looking for problems or faults

articles.questionB1: If you paid for a game and the publishers shut it down forever, would you sign a campaign to protect consumers like you? Why?
articles.questionB2: Given that the Stop Killing Games movement is gaining traction across Europe, should regulators scrutinise all digital purchases, beyond just games, to better protect consumer ownership rights?

articles.title: Armenia's pro-West government wins election despite Russian pressure
articles.summaryB1: Armenia held a parliamentary election recently, and the result was a clear victory for Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and his party, Civil Contract. The party won nearly 50% of the vote, which means it beat all the other contenders by a large amount. This was an important election because Armenia has been under a lot of pressure from Russia. Armenia used to be very close to Russia, but in recent years, Pashinyan has tried to move his country closer to the West, including the European Union and the United States. Russia was not happy about this change in direction and tried to influence the situation. However, Armenian voters chose to support Pashinyan anyway. This result shows that many people in Armenia want a future that is more connected to Western countries. Armenia is a small country in the South Caucasus region, between Europe and Asia. It has had many difficulties in recent years, including a military conflict with its neighbour Azerbaijan over a territory called Nagorno-Karabakh. The election result is significant because it gives Pashinyan a strong mandate to continue his pro-Western policies. Many people are watching closely to see how Russia will react and what this means for the wider region.

vocabularyB1.definition: People or groups competing against each other to win something
Attempts to force or influence someone to do something
To have an effect on how someone thinks or what they decide
Important and worth paying attention to
Official permission from voters to carry out a plan or policy

articles.summaryB2: Armenia's Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has secured a resounding electoral victory, with his Civil Contract Party claiming nearly 50% of the vote and comfortably outpacing all rival contenders. The result is widely seen as a strong public endorsement of Pashinyan's increasingly pro-Western foreign policy trajectory, which has placed him on a collision course with Moscow in recent years. Armenia, traditionally within Russia's sphere of influence, has been drifting steadily towards the European Union and the United States under Pashinyan's leadership, a geopolitical realignment that has drawn considerable ire from the Kremlin. Despite sustained Russian pressure aimed at swaying the outcome, Armenian voters delivered an unambiguous verdict in favour of deeper Western integration. The backdrop to this election is one of significant regional turbulence. Armenia suffered a humiliating military defeat in the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh war against Azerbaijan, and Pashinyan faced fierce domestic criticism over his handling of the conflict. Yet rather than capitalising on this vulnerability, his opponents failed to mount a credible challenge. The outcome carries broader implications for post-Soviet geopolitics, signalling that Russian leverage over former satellite states may be waning. For the European Union, the result presents a diplomatic opportunity to deepen ties with Yerevan, while Moscow faces the uncomfortable prospect of losing yet another neighbour to Western influence.

vocabularyB2.definition: Very clear and impressive, leaving no room for doubt
A significant shift in a country's political relationships and alliances internationally
Strong anger or displeasure
Gradually becoming weaker, smaller, or less powerful
Taking advantage of a situation or opportunity to gain benefit

articles.questionB1: Armenia's voters chose a pro-Western future despite strong pressure from Russia. Do you think small countries should have the freedom to choose their own alliances? Why?
articles.questionB2: With Russian influence waning across former Soviet states, do you think Armenia's geopolitical realignment will inspire similar shifts in neighbouring countries, or could it provoke a dangerous backlash from Moscow?

articles.title: Spain's visitor numbers hit new highs as tourists avoid Middle East
articles.summaryB1:
Spain has broken a record for tourism. In April 2024, the country welcomed 9.1 million international visitors. This is the highest number ever recorded for the month of April. It is a very positive sign for Spain's tourist industry.

One important reason for this increase is the situation in the Middle East. Because of conflict in that region, many tourists have decided to avoid travelling there. Instead, they are choosing safer destinations in Europe, and Spain is one of the most popular choices.

Spain is already one of the most visited countries in the world. It attracts tourists because of its warm weather, beautiful beaches, historic cities, and delicious food. Places like Barcelona, Madrid, and the Canary Islands are especially popular.

The record numbers are good news for the Spanish economy. Tourism creates many jobs and brings a lot of money into the country. Hotels, restaurants, and transport companies all benefit when more visitors arrive.

However, some people are concerned about the impact of so many tourists. In some cities, local residents have complained that tourism makes housing more expensive and public spaces more crowded. Balancing the benefits and problems of tourism is a challenge that Spain will need to manage carefully in the future.

vocabularyB1.definition: The highest or best result ever achieved in something
Places where people travel to on holiday or for a trip
Makes people want to come to a place or be interested in something
To gain something positive or useful from a situation
People who live permanently in a particular place

articles.summaryB2:
Spain has set a new benchmark in international tourism, recording 9.1 million foreign visitors in April 2024 — the highest figure ever for that month. The milestone underscores the country's enduring appeal as one of Europe's premier travel destinations, even as the global tourism landscape continues to shift dramatically.

A significant driver behind the surge appears to be ongoing instability in the Middle East. With conflict deterring travellers from visiting popular destinations in that region, many tourists have redirected their plans towards Mediterranean Europe, with Spain emerging as a clear beneficiary. This trend reflects a broader pattern of demand displacement, whereby geopolitical tensions in one region channel tourist flows towards perceived safer alternatives.

For the Spanish economy, the implications are largely positive. Tourism is a cornerstone of the country's GDP, supporting hundreds of thousands of jobs across hospitality, transport, and retail sectors. Record visitor numbers translate directly into increased revenue for businesses and greater tax receipts for the government.

Nevertheless, the boom is not without controversy. Anti-tourism sentiment has been growing in several Spanish cities, where residents argue that mass tourism inflates housing costs, strains public infrastructure, and erodes local culture. Protests have taken place in destinations such as Barcelona and the Canary Islands.

Spain therefore faces a delicate balancing act: capitalising on its extraordinary appeal to international visitors while addressing the legitimate concerns of the communities that host them.

vocabularyB2.definition: A standard or reference point used to measure achievement or performance
Discouraging or preventing someone from doing something, often through fear or difficulty
A person, group, or country that gains an advantage from a particular situation
The movement of something from its usual place to another, here referring to tourist demand shifting
Gradually destroys or weakens something over time

articles.questionB1: Spain attracts millions of tourists every year. Do you think record visitor numbers bring more benefits or problems for local residents?
articles.questionB2: With anti-tourism protests growing, how should Spain balance capitalising on its status as a key beneficiary of demand displacement while protecting the communities that host visitors?

articles.title: Exploding rocket casts doubts over Nasa's Moon plans
articles.summaryB1:
A large rocket built by a company called Blue Origin exploded during a test. This is bad news for both Blue Origin and for Nasa, the American space agency. Nasa had chosen Blue Origin to help build a special spacecraft that would land astronauts on the Moon. This is part of Nasa's Artemis programme, which plans to send humans back to the Moon for the first time in more than fifty years.

The rocket that exploded is called New Glenn. It was being tested when something went wrong and it was destroyed. Nobody was hurt because there were no people on board. However, the accident is a serious setback for the programme. A setback means something that slows down your progress or makes your plans more difficult.

Blue Origin is owned by Jeff Bezos, who also started the online shopping company Amazon. The company has been working hard to compete with other private space companies, such as SpaceX.

Nasa is already facing delays with its Moon mission. This explosion makes the situation more difficult. Scientists and engineers will need to investigate what went wrong before the rocket can be used again. Many people are now asking whether Nasa will be able to send astronauts to the Moon on schedule. The coming months will be very important for the future of this ambitious space programme.

vocabularyB1.definition: Burst suddenly with a loud noise and was completely destroyed
Something that causes delay or makes a plan more difficult to achieve
People who are trained to travel and work in space
To examine something carefully to find out what happened or why
Requiring a lot of effort and skill; involving big and difficult goals

articles.summaryB2:
An explosion involving a Blue Origin rocket has cast serious doubts over Nasa's already troubled plans to return astronauts to the Moon. The incident represents a significant blow to Jeff Bezos's space company, which had secured a contract with Nasa to develop a lunar lander as part of the agency's Artemis programme — an initiative designed to put humans back on the lunar surface for the first time since 1972.

The rocket destroyed in the explosion is New Glenn, Blue Origin's flagship launch vehicle. While no crew members were on board and there were no reported casualties, the loss of the vehicle is a considerable technical and financial setback. Engineers will now need to conduct a thorough investigation to determine the root cause of the failure before flight operations can resume.

The explosion compounds the difficulties already facing Nasa's Moon programme, which has endured repeated delays and rising costs. Critics have long questioned whether the agency's timeline is realistic, and this latest mishap is likely to intensify that scrutiny. Blue Origin has been striving to establish itself as a credible competitor in an increasingly crowded commercial space sector, where SpaceX has long dominated.

The broader implications extend beyond one company's fortunes. A prolonged grounding of New Glenn could disrupt the development schedule for the lunar lander, potentially pushing back the anticipated Moon landing date and raising further questions about Nasa's capacity to deliver on its commitments.

vocabularyB2.definition: To make people question whether something will succeed or is true
The most important or most advanced product or project of an organisation
Makes an already difficult problem worse by adding to it
Very careful and critical examination or attention from others
A long period during which aircraft or rockets are not allowed to fly

articles.questionB1: If you were a Nasa scientist, how would you investigate what caused the explosion, and do you think this setback will stop humans from reaching the Moon?
articles.questionB2: To what extent does the prolonged grounding of New Glenn cast serious doubts over Nasa's ability to meet its Artemis deadlines, and what alternatives might the agency consider?

articles.title: Spyro the Dragon returns with a new game after almost two decades
articles.summaryB1:
Spyro the Dragon is coming back! A new video game called Spyro: A Realm Beyond was recently announced. This is exciting news for many people who grew up playing games in the 1990s. The game is being made by a studio called Toys for Bob, based in California, USA. It will be available in spring 2027 on several platforms, including Xbox, PlayStation 5, PC, and Nintendo Switch 2.

Spyro is a purple dragon who first appeared on the PlayStation console in the late 1990s. He quickly became a popular mascot for a whole generation of young gamers. However, the last original Spyro game came out in 2008, so fans have been waiting a long time for something new.

In this new game, Spyro has a fresh new look but still has his trademark purple colour and iconic hairstyle. The original voice actor, Tom Kenny, is returning to give Spyro his voice. One exciting feature is that players can now fly freely at any time. The creative director explained that players can dive, flap their wings, and even use fire-breath to interact with the environment. The developers want the game to inspire feelings of joy and fun. This announcement has made many nostalgic fans very happy.

vocabularyB1.definition: A character or animal that represents a group, team, or product
A gaming system or device, such as PlayStation or Xbox, that you play games on
An important or interesting part of something
To communicate with or have an effect on something or someone
Feeling happy when you remember good things from the past

articles.summaryB2:
After nearly two decades of absence, Spyro the Dragon is set to make a triumphant return to gaming screens. Spyro: A Realm Beyond, developed by California-based studio Toys for Bob, was unveiled at Xbox's annual Game Showcase and is scheduled for release in spring 2027 across Xbox, PlayStation 5, PC, and Nintendo Switch 2.

The announcement marks a significant cultural moment. As gaming's most beloved millennial mascots have been systematically resuscitated — from Crash Bandicoot to Sonic — Spyro had remained conspicuously absent from the nostalgia-driven revival wave sweeping the industry. The last original title in the franchise dates back to 2008, making this new release long overdue for a devoted fanbase.

While the game preserves Spyro's trademark aesthetic, including his iconic purple colouring and distinctive quiff, it introduces meaningful mechanical innovations. Most notably, players can take flight at any time, a departure from the more constrained movement of the original titles. Creative director Lou Studdert emphasised that the team is leaning into the authentic fantasy of dragon gameplay: dynamic aerial manoeuvres, strategic use of fire-breath to manipulate the environment, and momentum-based flying mechanics all feature prominently.

Voice actor Tom Kenny, who originated the role, is reprising his performance — a detail likely to resonate strongly with long-term fans. With its stated ambition to inspire love, joy and laughter, the project positions itself not merely as a sequel, but as a heartfelt tribute to a defining era of gaming culture.

vocabularyB2.definition: Brought back to life or activity after a long period of being forgotten or inactive
In a way that is very easy to notice; obviously or remarkably
A clear change or move away from what was done before
Performing or taking on a role again that you did previously
Skilful or controlled movements, especially ones requiring careful planning or coordination

articles.questionB1: Spyro was a popular mascot for many gamers in the 1990s. Why do you think nostalgic feelings make people excited about old games returning?
articles.questionB2: With beloved franchises being resuscitated across the industry, do you think reprising original voice actors and classic aesthetics is enough to satisfy modern gaming audiences, or must developers innovate further?

articles.title: Trump to meet AI leaders to discuss US investment in their companies
articles.summaryB1:
US President Donald Trump has announced that he plans to meet with the leaders of some of the biggest artificial intelligence companies in the United States next week. The meetings are expected to focus on investment in these AI companies, which means the government may give or encourage large amounts of money to help them grow.

Artificial intelligence, or AI, is technology that allows computers to think and learn in ways that are similar to humans. It is used in many areas of daily life, such as search engines, healthcare, and transport. AI is one of the fastest-growing industries in the world right now.

The US government is very interested in making sure that America stays ahead in the global AI race, especially compared to countries like China. By meeting with AI leaders, Trump wants to show that his administration supports the technology sector and wants to attract more business to the country.

This kind of high-level meeting between a president and company leaders is significant because it can lead to big changes in how money is spent and how new technology is developed. It also sends a message to the rest of the world that the US sees AI as a national priority. Many people are watching these developments closely, as decisions made now could shape the future of technology for years to come.

vocabularyB1.definition: Money put into something to help it grow and make a profit later.
Computer technology that can think, learn, and solve problems like humans.
The group of people who run a country's government under a president.
Something that is considered more important than other things.
Important and likely to have a noticeable effect or meaning.

articles.summaryB2:
President Donald Trump announced on Friday that he intends to convene meetings with the chief executives of leading artificial intelligence companies in the coming week, with discussions expected to centre on US investment in their respective organisations. While details remain scarce, the announcement signals the administration's intent to position itself as a key stakeholder in the rapidly evolving AI landscape.

The move reflects a broader strategic imperative: ensuring American dominance in a sector increasingly viewed as central to both economic competitiveness and national security. Washington's growing preoccupation with AI is set against a backdrop of intensifying rivalry with China, whose own AI industry has made considerable strides in recent years. By engaging directly with industry titans, Trump appears eager to demonstrate that his administration is actively fostering the conditions for technological leadership.

Critics, however, may question the implications of such close ties between the executive branch and powerful private companies. Concerns around regulatory capture — where industries gain undue influence over the bodies meant to oversee them — are likely to resurface in this context.

From a business perspective, high-level government endorsement can accelerate funding, reduce regulatory friction, and attract international talent. For AI firms, proximity to political power carries both opportunity and scrutiny. As governments worldwide grapple with how to regulate transformative technologies, the outcomes of these meetings could have far-reaching consequences for the future trajectory of AI development in the United States and beyond.

vocabularyB2.definition: To formally arrange and bring together a meeting or group of people.
Something that is absolutely necessary or urgently required.
When an industry gains too much influence over the government bodies that regulate it.
The path or direction in which something develops over time.
Encouraging or helping something to develop and grow.

articles.questionB1: Why do you think investment in artificial intelligence has become such a big priority for governments around the world?
articles.questionB2: If regulatory capture becomes a real risk when governments convene closely with AI companies, what safeguards should be in place to protect the public interest?

articles.title: Zelensky's close European allies set out five conditions for peace talks
articles.summaryB1: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky recently met with some of Europe's strongest supporters of Ukraine. Together, they agreed on five conditions that must be met before peace talks with Russia can begin. These conditions are designed to protect Ukraine and make sure any agreement is fair and lasting. The meeting was very important because it showed that European countries are still strongly behind Ukraine, even as the situation in world politics is changing. At the same time, US President Donald Trump is now paying more attention to the conflict between the US and Iran. This means that Europe may need to take a bigger role in supporting Ukraine going forward. The war in Ukraine has been going on since Russia invaded the country in February 2022. Many people have died and millions have had to leave their homes. Peace talks have been discussed many times, but so far no agreement has been reached. Ukraine and its allies want to make sure that any peace deal does not reward Russia for its actions. The five conditions show that Ukraine is not willing to accept just any agreement. European leaders want to stay united and keep their support strong. This story matters because the decisions made now could shape the future of the war and the safety of Europe.

vocabularyB1.definition: Things that must happen or be agreed before something else can take place.
Countries or people who support and work together with another country or person.
A serious fight or war between two or more groups or countries.
Entered another country by force, using military power, without permission.
Working together as one group and agreeing on the same goals.

articles.summaryB2: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky convened a high-level meeting with his staunchest European allies to establish five key conditions that must be satisfied before any peace negotiations with Russia can begin. The summit underscored Europe's continued commitment to Ukraine at a diplomatically sensitive moment, as US President Donald Trump appears to be redirecting his administration's focus towards the escalating standoff with Iran. This potential shift in Washington's priorities has raised concerns among European capitals about the sustainability of American backing for Kyiv, prompting allies to reaffirm their own resolve. The five conditions put forward are intended to serve as a framework ensuring that any future settlement is both just and durable, rather than one that would effectively legitimise Russian territorial gains. Analysts suggest that by articulating clear prerequisites, Ukraine and its partners are attempting to retain leverage in any eventual diplomatic process and prevent a rushed or coerced agreement. The move also reflects growing European assertiveness in shaping the trajectory of the conflict, particularly as transatlantic unity faces new pressures. With the war now in its fourth year and no credible ceasefire in sight, the publication of these conditions signals that Kyiv and its allies remain unwilling to engage in talks without robust guarantees. The outcome of this diplomatic positioning could prove decisive in determining both the terms of a future peace and the long-term security architecture of the European continent.

vocabularyB2.definition: Formally brought together a group of people for an official meeting or discussion.
Conditions or requirements that must be met before something else can happen.
Confident, decisive behaviour in promoting one's own position or interests.
To make something appear acceptable, legal, or justified in the eyes of others.
Power or advantage that can be used to influence a situation or negotiation.

articles.questionB1: Why do you think Ukraine and its allies set conditions before agreeing to peace talks with Russia?
articles.questionB2: By publishing clear prerequisites for peace talks, do Ukraine and its allies gain real leverage, or does this assertiveness risk making a negotiated settlement harder to achieve?

articles.title: We need to stop AI developing without humans, says Anthropic co-founder
articles.summaryB1:
A well-known expert in artificial intelligence has warned that AI could soon develop on its own, without any help or control from humans. Jack Clark, one of the co-founders of Anthropic, a leading AI company, shared this concern in an interview with BBC's Newsnight programme.

Anthropic is one of the most important companies working on AI technology today. It was created by people who wanted to make sure AI develops in a safe and responsible way. Clark believes that if we are not careful, AI systems could reach a point where they improve and grow without human input. This means humans might lose control over how the technology changes.

This is a serious warning because AI is already being used in many areas of life, including medicine, business, and education. If AI starts to develop without human guidance, it could make decisions that affect people in ways that are difficult to predict or stop.

Clark's message is clear: we need to act now to make sure humans stay in control of AI development. He is calling on governments, companies, and scientists to work together to create better rules and safety systems. Many people agree that without proper oversight, the rapid growth of AI could bring serious risks to society. This story highlights why responsible AI development is so important.

vocabularyB1.definition: A person who starts a company or organisation together with one or more other people.
Computer systems that can do tasks that normally need human thinking, like learning or problem-solving.
Acting carefully and making good decisions that avoid harm to others.
Help, advice, or direction given to someone to support their actions or decisions.
The process of watching and checking something carefully to make sure it is done correctly.

articles.summaryB2:
Jack Clark, co-founder of the prominent AI safety company Anthropic, has issued a stark warning about the future trajectory of artificial intelligence. Speaking to BBC's Newsnight, Clark cautioned that AI technology could eventually reach a stage where it advances autonomously — that is, without any meaningful human input or supervision. This prospect raises profound questions about humanity's ability to retain control over one of the most transformative technologies ever developed.

Anthropic was established by former members of OpenAI with an explicit focus on building AI systems that are safe and aligned with human values. Despite this mission, Clark's comments suggest that even those closest to AI development harbour deep anxieties about where the technology is heading. His remarks reflect a growing consensus among researchers that the pace of AI progress may be outstripping our capacity to govern it effectively.

The implications of self-directed AI development are far-reaching. If systems begin to evolve beyond human understanding or control, the consequences for industries, governments, and individuals could be unpredictable and potentially irreversible. Critics argue that without robust regulatory frameworks, the competitive pressures driving AI innovation may override safety considerations.

Clark's intervention is therefore a call to action — urging policymakers, industry leaders, and the scientific community to collaborate on meaningful safeguards before it is too late. His warning underscores a broader debate about whether society is adequately prepared for the accelerating capabilities of modern AI.

vocabularyB2.definition: Acting independently, without control or direction from an outside person or system.
The path or direction in which something develops or progresses over time.
To hold or keep a feeling, thought, or doubt privately in your mind.
Growing or increasing faster than something else, leaving it behind.
Rules, systems, or actions designed to protect people from danger or harm.

articles.questionB1: If AI can develop without human guidance, what responsibilities do governments and companies have to keep oversight of the technology?
articles.questionB2: Given that even Anthropic's co-founder appears to harbour doubts about AI's trajectory, how confident can we be that existing safeguards are sufficient to prevent autonomous development?

articles.title: Astronauts return to ISS after sheltering during air leak repair attempt
articles.summaryB1: Astronauts on the International Space Station (ISS) had to move to a safe area while Russian crew members tried to fix an air leak in a tunnel section of the station. The ISS is a large spacecraft where astronauts from different countries live and work together in space. An air leak means that air is slowly escaping from part of the station, which can be dangerous for the people inside. During the repair attempt, five astronauts were told to shelter in a protected part of the station. This is a standard safety procedure used when there is a potential risk onboard. The Russian team worked to seal the damaged area and stop the leak. After the repair attempt was completed, all five astronauts were able to return to the main areas of the station. Keeping the ISS safe is very important because astronauts depend on the station's air supply to survive. Air leaks on space stations are not common, but they do happen from time to time. Engineers on the ground and the crew onboard work closely together to deal with these problems quickly. This event reminds us how challenging and sometimes dangerous life in space can be, even during routine operations.

vocabularyB1.definition: To move to a safe, protected place to avoid danger
To fix something that is broken or damaged
To close something tightly so that air or liquid cannot escape
An official set of steps followed to deal with a situation
An amount of something available for use when needed

articles.summaryB2: Five astronauts aboard the International Space Station were required to take refuge in a designated safe haven while Russian cosmonauts carried out an attempt to repair an air leak detected in one of the station's tunnel sections. The incident triggered a precautionary protocol, temporarily restricting the crew's access to certain areas of the station as a safeguard against any sudden deterioration in conditions. Air leaks, though relatively rare, pose a significant threat to the integrity of the ISS and the wellbeing of its inhabitants, since the station's pressurised environment is essential for survival in the vacuum of space. Russian engineers, both onboard and coordinating from the ground, worked methodically to identify and address the source of the leak. Once the repair attempt had been completed and the situation was deemed sufficiently stable, the five astronauts were cleared to return to the main sections of the station. The episode highlights the inherent hazards of long-duration spaceflight and underscores the critical importance of rapid, well-rehearsed emergency responses in an environment where mistakes can have severe consequences. It also draws attention to the ongoing operational challenges facing the ageing ISS, which relies on continuous maintenance to remain functional. International cooperation between crew members and ground teams remains a cornerstone of station safety.

vocabularyB2.definition: To move to a safe place in order to escape from danger
An official procedure followed in advance to prevent possible harm or risk
The process of becoming worse or more dangerous over time
Dangers that are a natural, unavoidable part of a situation or activity
The most important part of something that everything else depends on

articles.questionB1: If you had to follow a safety procedure during an emergency, how would you feel, and why is it essential to have a clear plan?
articles.questionB2: Given the inherent hazards of long-duration spaceflight, how effectively do you think international cooperation acts as a cornerstone for managing crises aboard the ageing ISS?

articles.title: Israel and Iran trade air strikes as ceasefire falters
articles.summaryB1:
Israel and Iran have attacked each other with missiles and drones in a new exchange of air strikes. This has put a ceasefire agreement, which started about two months ago, in serious danger. A ceasefire is an agreement to stop fighting, but both countries are now breaking it with these attacks.

The situation is also making things more difficult for US President Donald Trump, who has been trying to negotiate a bigger peace deal in the region. A deal like this would affect many countries in the Middle East, so the new violence is very worrying for diplomats and world leaders.

Israel and Iran have been enemies for many years. They disagree strongly about politics, religion, and power in the Middle East. In the past year, they have attacked each other directly several times, which is unusual because for a long time their conflict was indirect, fought through other groups.

The new strikes are called retaliatory, which means each side says it is responding to something the other side did first. This makes it very hard to stop the cycle of violence.

For ordinary people in the region, the threat of war is frightening. For the rest of the world, rising tension between two powerful countries with large militaries is a serious concern. Many people hope that a lasting agreement can still be reached before the situation gets worse.

vocabularyB1.definition: An agreement between two sides to stop fighting for a period of time
To talk with others to try to reach an agreement
Done as a response or punishment for something the other side did first
A serious disagreement or fight, often between countries or groups
A feeling of stress or worry caused by a difficult or dangerous situation

articles.summaryB2:
A fragile two-month ceasefire between Israel and Iran has been thrown into serious doubt after both countries exchanged retaliatory barrages of missiles and drones, dramatically escalating a conflict that has destabilised the broader Middle East for months. Each side claims its strikes were a direct response to the other's aggression, creating a dangerous cycle that diplomats fear could spiral into full-scale confrontation.

The renewed hostilities represent a significant setback for US President Donald Trump, who has been attempting to broker a sweeping regional deal that would reshape security arrangements across the Middle East. The collapse of the truce — or even its continued erosion — would substantially undermine those diplomatic ambitions, complicating Washington's ability to position itself as a credible mediator.

Israel and Iran have long waged a so-called shadow war, using proxy forces and covert operations rather than direct military engagement. However, the past year has seen an unprecedented shift toward open confrontation, with both nations launching direct strikes on each other's territory on multiple occasions.

Analysts warn that without a robust and enforceable framework, ceasefires between the two adversaries are inherently unstable. The latest exchange signals not only a failure of the current truce but also the broader difficulty of achieving durable peace in a region defined by deep ideological, geopolitical, and sectarian rivalries. International observers are urging renewed diplomatic intervention before the situation deteriorates beyond recovery.

vocabularyB2.definition: Easily broken or damaged; used here to mean an agreement that could fail easily
To arrange or negotiate a deal or agreement between two or more parties
Armed groups that fight on behalf of a more powerful country without direct involvement
A neutral party that helps two sides in a dispute reach an agreement
Long-lasting and able to survive difficulties; not easily ended or broken

articles.questionB1: Why do you think retaliatory strikes make a ceasefire so difficult to maintain, and who do you think should try to stop the conflict?
articles.questionB2: Given that ceasefires between these adversaries have proven fragile, what conditions would need to exist for a mediator like the US to broker a truly durable agreement?

articles.title: 'A World Cup for them not us': Fans' anger at US travel bans and visa restrictions
articles.summaryB1: The 2026 FIFA World Cup will be held in the United States, Canada, and Mexico. It is one of the biggest sports events in the world, and millions of football fans want to travel to watch the games. However, many fans are angry because they cannot get permission to enter the United States. The US government has strict travel bans and visa rules that stop people from certain countries from visiting. A visa is an official document that allows you to enter a foreign country. Fans from countries affected by these bans say they feel excluded from the tournament. They believe the World Cup should be open to everyone, not just people from countries that have good relations with the US. Some fans have described the situation as unfair and deeply disappointing. Football supporters around the world have spoken out about this issue, saying it is wrong to hold a global event in a country where so many people are not welcome. FIFA, the organisation that runs world football, has faced questions about whether it made the right choice by selecting the US as a host country. For many fans, this World Cup feels like it was made for some people, but not for others. The situation has caused a lot of frustration and anger in the international football community.

vocabularyB1.definition: Official approval that allows you to do something or go somewhere
An official document allowing you to enter or stay in a foreign country
Not allowed to join or take part in something; left out
A sports competition where many teams play to find the best one
The feeling of being upset because you cannot do what you want

articles.summaryB2: The 2026 FIFA World Cup, co-hosted by the United States, Canada, and Mexico, is supposed to be a celebration of global football. Yet for vast numbers of fans, it is shaping up to be anything but inclusive. Supporters from countries subject to US travel bans and stringent visa restrictions say they feel systematically excluded from an event that markets itself as uniting the world through sport. The discontent is not merely logistical. Many fans view the situation as a fundamental contradiction: a tournament with global pretensions being staged in a country that actively bars entry to citizens of numerous nations. Critics argue that FIFA, football's governing body, failed to adequately scrutinise the implications of awarding hosting rights to the US at a time of increasingly restrictive immigration policy. The anger has been particularly acute among fans from Muslim-majority countries and other nations targeted by Washington's travel regulations. For them, obtaining a visa is not a bureaucratic inconvenience but an insurmountable barrier. Several supporters have described the World Cup as being designed for wealthy, passport-privileged fans rather than the global working-class base that sustains football culture. FIFA has so far offered little in the way of concrete reassurance, drawing accusations of prioritising commercial interests over the sport's inclusive values. The episode raises uncomfortable questions about the ethics of hosting mega-events in countries with exclusionary immigration frameworks.

vocabularyB2.definition: Very strict and demanding, leaving little room for flexibility or exceptions
A feeling of dissatisfaction and unhappiness about a situation
To examine something very carefully and critically in great detail
Impossible to overcome or deal with successfully
Deliberately designed to keep certain people out or prevent their participation

articles.questionB1: If you wanted to attend a tournament but were excluded because of your nationality, how would you feel and what would you do?
articles.questionB2: To what extent did FIFA fail to scrutinise the exclusionary immigration policies of the US before awarding it hosting rights for a supposedly global event?

articles.title: Trump says Netanyahu will have ‘no choice’ but to accept a deal with Iran
articles.summaryB1: US President Donald Trump has said that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will have no choice but to accept a peace deal with Iran. Trump made these comments in an interview with the Financial Times. He said that he is the one who makes the important decisions, telling the newspaper that he 'calls the shots' when it comes to relations between the United States and other countries in the Middle East. Trump has been urging Netanyahu not to retaliate against Iran, meaning he does not want Israel to attack Iran in response to earlier actions. This is important because tensions between Israel and Iran have been very high recently, and many people are worried about a larger conflict starting in the region. Trump believes that a deal between Iran and Israel is the best way to bring peace and stability to the area. Netanyahu has not yet publicly agreed to follow Trump's advice, but Trump seems confident that the Israeli leader will eventually accept the agreement. This situation matters because the United States plays a very powerful role in Middle East politics, and Trump's strong language shows that he wants to be in control of how the situation develops. Many people around the world are watching closely to see what happens next.

vocabularyB1.definition: To agree to take or receive something that is offered to you
To do something harmful to someone because they harmed you first
A feeling of worry and danger between people or countries who do not trust each other
A situation that is calm, safe, and not likely to change suddenly
Feeling sure that something will happen or that you can do something well

articles.summaryB2: Donald Trump has declared that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will have 'no choice' but to accept a prospective nuclear deal with Iran, signalling a striking assertion of American dominance over its closest Middle Eastern ally. Speaking to the Financial Times, the US president insisted that he 'calls the shots' in the region, a remark widely interpreted as a pointed rebuke to Netanyahu, whom Trump had previously urged to refrain from retaliating against Tehran following recent hostilities. The statement underscores a notable shift in Washington's approach, with Trump appearing to prioritise diplomatic engagement with Iran over unconditional support for Israeli military objectives. This puts the two leaders on a potential collision course, as Netanyahu has long advocated a hardline stance towards Iran and has shown little appetite for concessions. Critics argue that Trump's blunt rhetoric risks undermining the credibility of the US-Israel alliance, while supporters contend that Washington must exert firm leverage to prevent a broader regional escalation. The situation is further complicated by Iran's ongoing nuclear programme, which Israel regards as an existential threat. By publicly pressuring Netanyahu in this manner, Trump appears to be staking out a unilateral position ahead of any formal negotiations, raising questions about how much genuine diplomatic groundwork has been laid and whether such a deal is genuinely achievable.

vocabularyB2.definition: A confident and forceful statement or claim about something
A strong and official criticism directed at someone for their behaviour or actions
Things you agree to give up or accept in order to reach an agreement
A rapid increase in the seriousness or intensity of a conflict or problem
Done by only one country or person, without agreement from others involved

articles.questionB1: Do you think Netanyahu will accept a deal with Iran to bring stability to the region, or will tensions continue to grow?
articles.questionB2: To what extent does Trump's unilateral assertion that he 'calls the shots' risk damaging the US-Israel alliance and reducing America's credibility as a diplomatic partner?

articles.title: EU Plans Major Investment in Eastern European Transport Links
articles.summaryB1: The European Union is planning to spend a lot of money on roads and railways near its eastern borders. This will help countries like Poland, Lithuania and Romania to connect better with the rest of Europe. EU leaders agreed that better transport links are very important for the economy and for security. The money will come from a special EU fund. Work on the new roads and railways is expected to start next year. Many people who live near the border are happy about this decision. They hope that better infrastructure will also bring more jobs to their region. Poland will receive one of the largest shares of the total funding because it has a very long eastern border with Ukraine and Belarus. Local governments in Poland are already making detailed plans for how to use the money effectively.

vocabularyB1.definition: The basic systems a country needs, like roads, railways and power supplies
Money given for a specific purpose
Roads, railways and other connections that allow people to travel between places
A large area of a country with particular characteristics
In a way that works well and produces the right result

articles.summaryB2: The European Commission has unveiled a comprehensive package to bolster transport and logistical infrastructure along the EU's eastern flank, with particular emphasis on Poland, the Baltic states and Romania. The initiative draws on the Cohesion Fund and newly established defence-linked financing instruments, aiming to dual-purpose civilian infrastructure for potential military mobility requirements — a concept increasingly central to NATO's strategic posture. Poland stands to receive a disproportionately large allocation given the considerable extent of its eastern border with Ukraine and Belarus. Critics have raised legitimate questions about procurement timelines and the adequacy of environmental impact assessments, while several MEPs have called for greater transparency in the tendering process. Proponents argue that the security and economic rationale is compelling, particularly in the context of ongoing geopolitical uncertainty in the region.

vocabularyB2.definition: To strengthen or improve something significantly
Designed to serve two completely different functions at the same time
To a degree that is larger or smaller than would normally be expected
The formal procedure of inviting and selecting competitive bids for a contract
Relating to politics strongly influenced by geographical factors and international relations

articles.questionB1: How do you think better transport links and infrastructure could change daily life for people living in border regions of Poland or Romania?
articles.questionB2: Given the dual-purpose nature of this infrastructure funding, how effectively can the EU balance genuine civilian development needs against its evolving geopolitical and military mobility priorities?

articles.title: Tech Giants Face New EU Digital Rules From Autumn
articles.summaryB1: Big technology companies like Google and Meta will have to follow new rules in Europe from this autumn. The rules are part of a plan to make the internet safer and more fair for everyone. Companies that break the rules can be fined a lot of money — up to ten percent of their total income worldwide. European countries, including Poland, have strongly supported these new regulations. Users will have more control over their personal information and how large companies use it. The new rules also mean that big companies cannot use unfair methods to stop smaller companies from competing with them. Poland's digital ministry has been one of the most active supporters of strict enforcement of these rules. Many Polish internet users say they feel better protected by these changes.

vocabularyB1.definition: Official rules made by a government or authority that must be followed
The process of making sure that rules or laws are actually followed
Required to pay money as a punishment for breaking a rule or law
Trying to be more successful than others who are selling similar products or services
Kept safe from harm, danger or unfair treatment

articles.summaryB2: The Digital Markets Act enforcement timeline has been accelerated, with the European Commission confirming that designated 'gatekeepers' — including Alphabet, Meta and Apple — must demonstrate full compliance by October. The regulation targets anti-competitive behaviour, mandatory interoperability between platforms, and greater algorithmic transparency. Poland's digital ministry has been notably vocal in pushing for stricter enforcement mechanisms, reflecting broader Central European frustration with the perceived dominance of American platforms in local media ecosystems. Non-compliance carries penalties of up to 10% of global annual turnover, with repeat offenders potentially facing structural remedies including forced divestiture. Legal analysts widely expect several major platforms to challenge specific provisions in the Court of Justice of the EU.

vocabularyB2.definition: Companies that control access to important digital markets or platforms
The ability of different digital systems or applications to work together seamlessly
Making it clear and understandable how automated computer systems make decisions
The forced sale or disposal of a part of a business, often required by regulators
Specific conditions or requirements within a law or legal agreement

articles.questionB1: If big companies are fined for breaking these regulations, do you think smaller companies will truly get a fair chance to compete online?
articles.questionB2: Given that gatekeepers may challenge key provisions in court, how realistic is it to expect full compliance and meaningful algorithmic transparency by October?

articles.title: Central European Cities Plant Thousands of Trees to Beat the Heat
articles.summaryB1: Cities in Central Europe, including Warsaw and Prague, are planting many new trees and building parks to deal with very hot summers. Scientists say that cities are getting hotter because of climate change. Green spaces help to cool the air and make life more comfortable for people living there. Local governments are spending large amounts of money on these projects. In Warsaw, the city plans to plant thousands of new trees along busy streets over the next three years. Prague is also creating several new parks in areas where there were previously only buildings and concrete. Both cities say that green areas are not just nice to look at — they are necessary for people's health during periods of extreme heat. Residents in both cities say they are happy that their local governments are taking this problem seriously.

vocabularyB1.definition: Long-term changes in global temperatures and weather patterns, mainly caused by human activities
Temperatures that are much higher than usual and can be dangerous to people's health
People who live permanently in a particular place or area
A hard building material made from cement, sand and water, used for roads and buildings
At an earlier time; before the current situation existed

articles.summaryB2: Municipal authorities across Central Europe are implementing so-called 'sponge city' strategies as urban heat islands intensify under accelerating climate projections. Warsaw's latest urban masterplan earmarks 18% of all new development land for permeable surfaces and expanding tree canopy, while Kraków has introduced mandatory heat-resilience requirements into its building regulations. Urban planners acknowledge a fundamental tension between densification pressures — driven by acute housing shortages — and the ecological imperative to preserve green corridors that regulate urban microclimates. Research from the Warsaw University of Life Sciences suggests mature street trees can reduce local temperatures by up to 8°C on peak summer days, lending considerable scientific weight to what critics had previously dismissed as a purely aesthetic concern.

vocabularyB2.definition: City areas significantly warmer than surrounding rural areas due to buildings, roads and human activity
Ground surfaces that allow rainwater to pass through rather than run off into drains
The process of increasing the number of buildings and population density in an urban area
Climate conditions specific to a small local area, which may differ significantly from the wider region
Relating to beauty and visual appearance rather than practical usefulness

articles.questionB1: How do you think planting trees and creating green spaces can help residents stay healthy during periods of extreme heat in cities?
articles.questionB2: Given the tension between densification and preserving green corridors, how should city planners balance housing shortages with the need to reduce urban heat islands?

articles.title: European Central Bank Signals Cautious Approach to Interest Rates
articles.summaryB1: The European Central Bank says it will be very careful about changing interest rates this year. Interest rates affect how much it costs to borrow money from a bank. When rates are high, people pay more for mortgages and business loans. The bank is worried about inflation, which means the prices of everyday things going up faster than usual. Poland is not part of the eurozone and uses the zloty, but decisions made by the European Central Bank still have an important effect on Poland's economy. Many Polish businesses borrow money in euros, so changes in European interest rates affect them directly. Economists say that the bank wants to be sure that inflation is really under control before it makes any big changes. This cautious approach means that borrowing will remain expensive for some time.

vocabularyB1.definition: The percentage charged by a bank for lending money, or paid on savings
A general increase in prices over time, reducing what you can buy with the same amount of money
Loans taken from a bank to buy a house or flat, repaid over many years
The group of EU countries that use the euro as their currency
Being careful and not taking risks; not acting too quickly

articles.summaryB2: The ECB's governing council has signalled a more cautious approach to further monetary easing, citing persistent services inflation and wage growth that remains above pre-pandemic trends. The hawkish tone, communicated through President Christine Lagarde's carefully worded forward guidance, has prompted a modest repricing of rate expectations in European swap markets. For Poland and other non-eurozone Central European economies, the ECB's stance indirectly constrains the National Bank of Poland's room for manoeuvre, given the zloty's well-documented sensitivity to euro-area monetary conditions. Analysts at several Warsaw-based investment banks have consequently revised their forecasts for domestic rate cuts, pushing expected reductions further into the second half of the year.

vocabularyB2.definition: Central bank policy of reducing interest rates to stimulate economic activity and borrowing
Favouring higher interest rates and tighter monetary policy to control inflation
A central bank's communication about its likely future policy decisions to influence expectations
Adjusting the expected value or cost of financial instruments based on new information
Freedom or flexibility to act or make independent choices within constraints

articles.questionB1: If inflation is still high in Europe, do you think a cautious approach to changing interest rates is the right decision? Why?
articles.questionB2: Given the ECB's hawkish forward guidance, how much room for manoeuvre does the National Bank of Poland realistically have when deciding its own rate policy?

articles.title: Polish Film Industry Gains Growing International Recognition
articles.summaryB1: Polish films are becoming more popular and well-known around the world. Three Polish films have been selected for important international film festivals this year. Film-makers from Poland say they want to tell stories about Polish history and modern Polish life in ways that people from other countries can also understand and enjoy. Streaming services like Netflix are very interested in Polish content and are spending more money on Polish productions. More young people in Poland are now choosing to study film-making at university. Industry experts say that Polish cinema has a unique voice that audiences around the world are beginning to appreciate. Warsaw is becoming an increasingly important European centre for film and television production, attracting foreign productions that use Polish studios and local talent.

vocabularyB1.definition: Events where films from different countries are shown and sometimes given prizes
Films, TV shows or other media that have been made
Online platforms like Netflix where you can watch films and shows over the internet
Being the only one of its kind; unlike anything else
People with natural ability and skill in a particular area

articles.summaryB2: Poland's cinematic output is attracting sustained international attention, with three features shortlisted for major festivals including Venice and Toronto. Analysts attribute this momentum partly to co-production frameworks with German and French broadcasters, and partly to a generational shift in domestic storytelling — younger directors are engaging with post-communist memory and contemporary Polish identity in formally adventurous and internationally accessible ways. Netflix's Warsaw-based content team has reportedly doubled its commissioning budget for Polish-language originals, signalling growing confidence that Polish narratives can translate successfully across diverse global markets. Warsaw is increasingly positioning itself as a significant Central European production hub.

vocabularyB2.definition: The total number of films produced by a country or film-maker over a period of time
Included in a small final group of candidates being considered for a prize or selection
Formal agreements allowing companies from different countries to jointly finance and make films
Money set aside by a broadcaster or platform to order and pay for new original content
Relating to societies and culture in the period after communist rule ended in Eastern Europe

articles.questionB1: Which types of stories from Polish history or modern life do you think streaming services would find most interesting for global audiences, and why?
articles.questionB2: To what extent do co-production frameworks risk shaping Polish cinematic output to suit foreign market expectations rather than authentically reflecting post-communist identity?

articles.title: AI Tools Reshape Hiring Practices Across Europe
